HIS-17.quote: Cornwallis had also decreed that the zamindars should issue written agreements (called pattas) to each cultivator. In practice, however, no such pattas were issued, and the peasants were wholly at the mercy of the zamindars.

HIS-17.claim: Only in 1859 did the state take some step to protect tenants: a law that year gave limited protection to old tenants, now termed occupancy tenants.
HIS-17.quote: Only in 1859 did the State take some step to protect the rights of tenant: a law passed that year bestowed a limited protection on old tenants, who were now termed occupancy tenants.

HIS-17.claim: By 1820 the Madras authorities were converted to the ryotwari system, its triumph indicated by the appointment of Munro as Governor of Madras.
HIS-17.quote: the Madras authorities were by 1820 converted to the ryotwari system, and its triumph was indicated by the appointment of Munro as Governor of Madras.

HIS-17.claim: Ryotwari yielded a larger revenue than any other system because there were no zamindars or intermediaries taking a share of the agricultural surplus.
HIS-17.quote: Its adoption was due, however, to one main reason– it resulted in a larger revenue than any other system could have produced. This was because there were no zamindars or other intermediaries who received any part of the agricultural surplus

HIS-17.claim: The crops on which the Company concentrated were indigo, cotton, raw silk, opium and pepper, and in the nineteenth century also tea and sugar.
HIS-17.quote: The crops on which the company concentrated were indigo, cotton, raw silk, opium, pepper, and, in the 19th century, also tea and sugar.

HIS-17.claim: Company-era exports served to remit resources out of India — the Indian 'tribute' transferred to Britain; India received no imports in return, and such a transfer impoverished India.
HIS-17.quote: The exports therefore served essentially to remit resources out of India. It was the method by which the Indian 'tribute' was transferred to Britain. India received no imports in return for these exports. Obviously such a transfer impoverished India.

HIS-17.claim: The Charter Act of 1813 abolished the Company's monopoly in Indian trade; the Charter Act of 1833 abolished the remaining monopoly, that in the China trade.
HIS-17.quote: In these circumstances the Charter Act of 1813 was passed abolishing the monopoly in Indian trade; another Charter Act in 1833 abolished the remaining part of the Company's privileged monopoly, that in the China trade.

HIS-17.claim: The value of cotton cloth exported from India to England declined from £1.3 million to £0.1 million between 1815 and 1832, while imports of English cotton cloth into India increased almost 15 times.
HIS-17.quote: The value of cotton cloth exported from India to England declined from pound 1.3 million to only pound 0.1 million in the years 1815 to 1832. In the same period the import of cotton cloth from England increased almost 15 times.

HIS-17.claim: Revenue used to buy export goods (the so-called 'investment') was, as a House of Commons committee put it in 1783, merely a means of 'payment of a tribute' — a major example of what nationalists later called economic drain.
HIS-17.quote: such 'investment' was not actually employment of trading capital brought into Bengal, but merely a means of “payment of a tribute”. This was a major example of what the Indian economic nationalists later called 'economic drain'.

HIS-17.claim: On the evidence, the Indian manufacturing sector did decline in the face of competition from machine-made, technologically superior manufactured imports from Britain during the first century of colonial rule.
HIS-17.quote: we can safely conclude that the Indian manufacturing sector did decline in the face of completion from machine-made, technologically superior manufactured imports from Britain during the first century of colonial rule in India.

HIS-17.claim: In his 1867 paper 'England's Debt to India' Dadabhai Naoroji first highlighted that Britain was extracting more than one-fourth of India's revenue.
HIS-17.quote: In a paper entitled ‘England's Debt to India' Dadabhai Naoroji first highlighted in 1867 that Britain was bleeding India by extracting and appropriating more than one-fourth of India's revenue.

HIS-17.claim: Naoroji developed his argument in the 1873 paper 'Poverty of India' and in 1901 wrote Poverty and Un-British Rule in India.
HIS-17.quote: He developed his arguments further in a paper on the 'Poverty of India' in 1873 and in 1901 he wrote Poverty and Un-British Rule in India.

HIS-17.claim: Dadabhai Naoroji became the major proponent and propagator of the drain of wealth from India; for him the drain was also a loss of capital and the major cause of India's poverty.
HIS-17.quote: It is Dadabhai Naoroji who became the major proponent and propagator of the drain of wealth from India. It was not only about the loss of wealth but also about the loss of capital. It was the major cause of poverty in India.

HIS-17.claim: The widest definition of the drain was Naoroji's idea of an unrequited export surplus: India did not get an equivalent return in merchandise or treasure.
HIS-17.quote: The widest definition of the drain was based on Naoroji's ideas of an unrequited export surplus – that India did not get an equivalent return either in terms of merchandise or treasure.

HIS-17.claim: Home Charges were the sum remitted annually in sterling from India to Britain for the Government of India's expenses in Britain, pensions of civil and military officials, stores and private remittances.
HIS-17.quote: The narrower definition was that based on the Home Charges – the sum of money that had to be remitted annually in pound sterling from India to Britain. These charges were to pay for the expenses of the Government of India incurred in Britain, the payments due in Britain for the pensions of civil and military officials, the purchase of stores and private remittances by non-officials.

HIS-17.claim: Naoroji spoke of a 'moral drain': because Indians were excluded from higher positions, they could not develop higher skills and knowledge.
HIS-17.quote: This led to a ''moral drain'' since Indians could not develop higher skills and knowledge and those Europeans in India who did left the country after retirement.

HIS-17.claim: Nationalists argued railway lines were laid to promote British industries — to move cotton goods from ports to consuming centres and raw cotton from the interior to port towns.
HIS-17.quote: The railway lines were laid to promote the interest of the British industries – to move cotton goods from the ports to consuming centres and to move raw cotton from the interior to the port towns.

HIS-17.claim: At the beginning of the twentieth century R.C. Dutt estimated the drain at twenty million pounds a year.
HIS-17.quote: At the beginning of the twentieth century R.C. Dutt estimated the drain at twenty million pounds a year.

HIS-17.claim: In response to peasant demands to regulate tenancy, the government passed the Bengal Tenancy Act in 1885, which gave some protection to tenants.
HIS-17.quote: In response to the demands of the peasants to regulate the system of tenancy the government passed the Bengal Tenancy Act in 1885 which gave some form of protection to the tenants.

HIS-17.claim: In Pabna the landlords increased rents seven-fold during the period from 1793 to 1872.
HIS-17.quote: Many peasants here had occupancy rights which protected them against arbitrary eviction by the landlords. However the rent was fixed by the landlords who increased it seven fold during the period from 1793 to 1872.

HIS-17.claim: In 1879 the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act was passed, giving peasants legal remedies against unreasonable demands of moneylenders.
HIS-17.quote: In 1879 the Deccan Agriculturalists' Relief Act was passed which gave relief to the peasant by making available legal remedies to counter unreasonable demands.

HIS-27.claim: The Regulating Act of 1773 was Parliament's first important Act to control the Company's administration.
HIS-27.quote: the Parliament passed its first important Act in 1773. called the Regulating Act to control the Company's Administration.

HIS-27.claim: Under the Regulating Act the Governor of Bengal was raised to Governor General, with a Council of four members, controlling Madras and Bombay in war and peace.
HIS-27.quote: the status of Governor of Bengal was raised to Governor General. His Council would consist of four members. The Governor General in Council was given the power to superintend and control the presidencies of Madras and Bombay in matters of war and peace.

HIS-27.claim: The Regulating Act provided for a Supreme Court of Justice at Calcutta.
HIS-27.quote: The Act also provided for the establishment of a Supreme Court of Justice at Calcutta

HIS-27.claim: The Regulating Act worked badly: the Governor General faced a united hostile council, had no power to override it, and only a casting vote on a tie.
HIS-27.quote: The Governor General had to face the opposition of his council, who united against him. He had no power to override them, though in case of an equal division he had a casting vote.

HIS-27.claim: Pitt's India Act was passed in August 1784 to remove the defects of the Regulating Act.
HIS-27.quote: Pitt's India Act was passed in August, 1784. The purpose was to remove defects in the Regulating Act.

HIS-27.claim: Pitt's Act set up a Board of Control of six commissioners including two Cabinet ministers, to control civil and military government of British territories in India.
HIS-27.quote: The Act established a Board of Control consisting of six commissioners, including, two Cabinet ministers. They were to control all matters of civil and military Government of the British territories in India.

HIS-27.claim: Pitt's Act placed India's government under the Governor General and a Council of three.
HIS-27.quote: the government of India be placed under the Governor General and a Council of three, so that if only one member of the Council supported him, he could have his way.

HIS-27.claim: Pitt's Act made Madras and Bombay subordinate to Bengal in war, diplomacy and revenue.
HIS-27.quote: The Act clearly stated that the Presidencies of Madras and Bombay were to be subordinate to the Presidency of Bengal in all matters of war, diplomatic relations and revenue.

HIS-27.claim: The Act of 1786 gave Cornwallis the power to override his council and united the offices of Governor General and Commander-in-Chief in one person.
HIS-27.quote: The Act of 1786 gave him the powers he asked for. The offices of the Governor General and the Commander-in-Chief were to be united in the same person.

HIS-27.claim: The Charter Act of 1793 renewed the Company's Charter for 20 years.
HIS-27.quote: The Charter of the Company was renewed for 20 years and it was declared that it would be allowed to continue with the possession of all territories for the next 20 years.

HIS-27.claim: The Act of 1793 laid the foundation of government by written laws and regulations in British India.
HIS-27.quote: The Act of 1793 thus laid the foundation of government by written laws and regulations in British India in place of the personal rule of the past rulers.

HIS-27.claim: The Charter Act of 1813 deprived the Company of its monopoly of trade with India, while it kept the China trade monopoly for 20 more years.
HIS-27.quote: The Company was deprived of its monopoly of trade with India. It was allowed to continue with its monopoly of trade with China for 20 years.

HIS-27.claim: The Charter Act of 1833 abolished the tea/China trade monopoly; the Company was left with only political functions.
HIS-27.quote: The monopoly of tea trade with China was abolished. The Company was to have only political functions.

HIS-27.claim: By the Act of 1833 the Governor General of Bengal became the Governor General of India.
HIS-27.quote: Governor General of Bengal became the Governor General of India.

HIS-27.claim: The Act of 1833 added a Law Member to the Governor General's Executive Council; Macaulay was the Law Member.
HIS-27.quote: The Act added one more member to the Executive council of the Governor General. the Law Member, whose work was fully legislative. Lord Macaulay, the Law member, influenced the educational policy of the government for a number of years.

HIS-27.claim: Section 87 of the Charter Act 1833 declared no Indian would be disqualified from Company service for religion, birth, descent or colour.
HIS-27.quote: Section 87 of the Act declared, "that no native or natural born subject of the crown resident in India should be by reason only of his religion, place of birth, descent, colour or any of them be disqualified for any place in the company's service."

HIS-27.claim: The Charter Act of 1853 carried the separation of executive and legislative functions further by adding members of council for legislation.
HIS-27.quote: By the Act of 1853, separation of the executive and the legislative functions was carried a step further by the provision of additional members of council for the purpose of legislation.

HIS-27.claim: Under the 1853 Act the central Legislative Council was to consist of 12 members, and legislation was for the first time treated as a special function of government.
HIS-27.quote: The Council in its legislative capacity was to consist of 12 members. The "Legislative Councillors" were neatly distinguished from the "Executive Councillors" and by doing so, legislation was for the first time treated as a special function of the government requiring special machinery and special procedure.

HIS-27.claim: The Charter Act of 1853 provided that all vacancies in India were to be filled by competitive examinations; Macaulay was appointed President of the Committee.
HIS-27.quote: All vacancies in India were to be filled in by competitive examinations. Lord Macaulay was appointed the President of the Committee.

HIS-27.claim: The Government of India Act became an Act of Parliament in August 1858 and the government of India passed from the Company to the Crown.
HIS-27.quote: Lord Stanley, President of the Board of Control introduced a bill for the 'Better Government' of India which became an Act of Parliament in August 1858. The Government of India passed from the hands of the English East India Company to the crown.

HIS-27.claim: The 1858 Act abolished the Board of Control and the Court of Directors; their place was taken by the Secretary of State for India and his India Council.
HIS-27.quote: The Board of control and court of Directors were abolished. Their place was taken by the Secretary of State of India and his India Council.

HIS-27.claim: After 1858 the Governor General became known as the Viceroy, the Crown's representative.
HIS-27.quote: The Governor General became known from now as the Viceroy or Crown's representative.

HIS-27.claim: Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General (1773-1785) and introduced administrative reforms, notably in justice.
HIS-27.quote: Warren Hastings (Governor-General from 1773 to 1785) was one of the many important figures who played a role in the expansion of Company power. The supreme head of the administration was the Governor-General. Warren Hastings, the first Governor-General, introduced several administrative reforms, notably in the sphere of justice.

HIS-27.claim: From 1772 each district was to have a criminal court (faujdari adalat) and a civil court (diwani adalat).
HIS-27.quote: From 1772 a new system of justice was established. Each district was to have two courts - a criminal court (faujdari adalat) and a civil court (diwani adalat).

HIS-27.claim: Hastings' impeachment proceeding in the British Parliament lasted seven years.
HIS-27.quote: When Warren Hastings went back to England in 1785, Edmund Burke accused him of being personally responsible for the misgovernment of Bengal. This led to an impeachment proceeding in the British Parliament that lasted seven years.

HIS-27.claim: Under the Regulating Act of 1773 a new Supreme Court was established at Calcutta, with the Sadar Nizamat Adalat as court of appeal.
HIS-27.quote: Under the Regulating Act of 1773, a new Supreme Court was established, while a court of appeal - the Sadar Nizamat Adalat - was also set up at Calcutta.

HIS-27.claim: The building of the administrative structure started taking shape from 1793 under Cornwallis, including the separation of judicial from executive functions.
HIS-27.quote: The building up of an adequate structure of administration started taking shape from 1793 under Cornwallis. These changes involved a divorce of revenue from civil administration, i.e., the separation of judicial from executive functions and the multiplication of judicial courts.

HIS-27.claim: Cornwallis tried to check civil servants' corruption by forbidding private trade and raising salaries in compensation.
HIS-27.quote: Cornwallis tried to check this corruption. He imposed certain restrictions on the civil servants (like forbiding private trade) but increased their salaries as a compensation.

HIS-27.claim: The police, the third pillar of British administration, was created by Cornwallis, organised into thanas headed by an Indian Daroga.
HIS-27.quote: Police, the third Pillar of the British administration was created by Cornwallis. This force was grouped into Thanas, headed by a Daroga who was an Indian.

HIS-27.claim: In 1793 it was officially laid down that all higher posts worth 500 a year or more could be held only by an Englishman.
HIS-27.quote: it had officially been laid down in 1793 that all higher posts in administration worth a salary of 500 a year or more could be held only by an Englishman.

HIS-27.claim: An East India College was established at Haileybury to give two years' training to young officers for the civil services.
HIS-27.quote: an East India College was established at Hailybury for imparting two years, training to young officers for the civil services.

HIS-27.claim: The idea of competition for recruitment was first introduced by the Charter Act of 1833, but only as limited nomination-cum-competition.
HIS-27.quote: The idea of 'competition' for recruitment (as against nomination practised earlier) was introduced for the first time by the Charter Act of 1833. But it was to be a very limited competition and could be termed as nomination-cum-competition.

HIS-27.claim: After 1853 open competition replaced nomination; Haileybury was abolished in 1858 and the examination, held annually in England, was virtually impossible for an Indian to compete in.
HIS-27.quote: The Charter Act of 1853 ultimately took away the power of the court of Directors to make nominations and made a provision for open competition. Subsequently the college at Hailybury was abolished in 1858 and the competitive examinations became the sole responsibility of the Civil Service Commission. This competitive examination was to be held annually in England and it was therefore, virtually impossible for an Indian to compete in it.

HIS-27.claim: It was left to Bentinck, the Governor-General, to legislate against widow burning (sati) in December 1829.
HIS-27.quote: Finally it was left to Bentinck, the Governor-General to legislate against Widow burning in December 1829.

HIS-27.claim: Rammohan Roy led the Westernised Bengali intelligentsia's agitation for abolition of sati and petitioned the government in 1818.
HIS-27.quote: the Westernized Bengali intelligentsia led by Rammohan Roy actively agitated for the abolition of Sati. In 1818 he sent a petition to the government urging them to abolish this practice

HIS-27.claim: Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General 1848-1856, devised the Doctrine of Lapse.
HIS-27.quote: The final wave of annexations occurred under Lord Dalhousie who was the Governor-General from 1848 to 1856. He devised a policy that came to be known as the Doctrine of Lapse.

HIS-27.claim: Under the Doctrine of Lapse a kingdom lapsed to the Company if a ruler died without a male heir: Satara (1848), Sambalpur (1850), Udaipur (1852), Nagpur (1853), Jhansi (1854).
HIS-27.quote: The doctrine declared that if an Indian ruler died without a male heir his kingdom would "lapse", that is, become a part of Company territory. One kingdom after another was annexed simply by applying this doctrine: Satara (1848), Sambalpur (1850), Udaipur (1852), Nagpur (1853) and Jhansi (1854).

HIS-27.claim: In 1856 the Company took over Awadh, claiming a duty to free its people from the Nawab's misgovernment.
HIS-27.quote: Finally, in 1856, the Company also took over Awadh. This time the British had an added argument - they said they were "obliged by duty" to take over Awadh in order to free the people from the "misgovernment" of the Nawab.

HIS-27.claim: In 1856 Governor-General Canning decided Bahadur Shah Zafar would be the last Mughal king.
HIS-27.quote: In 1856, Governor-General Canning decided that Bahadur Shah Zafar would be the last Mughal king and after his death none of his descendants would be recognised as kings

HIS-27.claim: The massive uprising against the Company started in May 1857.
HIS-27.quote: the English East India Company faced a massive uprising that started in May 1857 and threatened the Company's very presence in India.

HIS-27.claim: A subsidiary alliance was imposed on Awadh in 1801 and it was taken over in 1856; Dalhousie declared it misgoverned.
HIS-27.quote: Awadh was one of the last territories to be annexed. In 1801, a subsidiary alliance was imposed on Awadh, and in 1856 it was taken over. Governor-General Dalhousie declared that the territory was being misgoverned and British rule was needed to ensure proper administration.

HIS-27.claim: Under Lord Hastings (Governor-General 1813-1823) the policy of paramountcy was initiated.
HIS-27.quote: Under Lord Hastings (Governor-General from 1813 to 1823), a new policy of "paramountcy" was initiated. Now the Company claimed that its authority was paramount or supreme

HIS-27.claim: The Arms Act and the Vernacular Press Act were both passed in 1878; the VPA aimed to silence critics of the government.
HIS-27.quote: The Arms Act was passed in 1878, disallowing Indians from possessing arms. In the same year, the Vernacular Press Act was also enacted in an effort to silence those who were critical of the government.

HIS-27.claim: The Vernacular Press Act allowed the government to confiscate newspapers' assets including printing presses for objectionable publication.
HIS-27.quote: The Act allowed the government to confiscate the assets of newspapers including their printing presses if the newspapers published anything that was found "objectionable".

HIS-27.claim: The Ilbert Bill (1883) provided for trial of British/European persons by Indian judges and sought equality between British and Indian judges; white opposition forced its withdrawal in original form.
HIS-27.quote: In 1883, there was a furore over the attempt by the government to introduce the Ilbert Bill. The bill provided for the trial of British or European persons by Indians, and sought equality between British and Indian judges in the country. But when white opposition forced the government to withdraw the bill, Indians were enraged.

HIS-27.claim: During Lytton's period the maximum age for the Indian Civil Service examination was reduced from 21 to 19 years.
HIS-27.quote: During his period the maximum age for appearing in the Indian Civil Service examination was reduced from 21 to 19 years.

HIS-27.claim: Under Lytton, public meetings protested the Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act; the VPA restricted newspapers printed in Indian languages, and the Amrita Bazar Patrika switched to English overnight to escape it.
HIS-27.quote: Public meetings were organised to protest against the passing of the Vernacular Press Act and the Arms Act. The former imposed restrictions on the newspapers and journals printed in Indian languages. Amrita Basar Patrika, which was published in Bengali till then, changed overnight into an English medium paper so as to escape the restrictions imposed under this Act.

HIS-27.claim: Lord Lytton was succeeded by Lord Ripon in 1880; Ripon repealed the Vernacular Press Act and promoted local self-government.
HIS-27.quote: Lord Lytton was succeeded by Lord Ripon in 1880. He repealed the Vernacular Press Act, promoted local self-government institutions, encouraged the spread of education and brought the Afghan War to an end.

HIS-27.claim: The Ilbert Bill was amended under Anglo-Indian pressure in such a manner that its very purpose was defeated.
HIS-27.quote: Ultimately the Government had to bow before this hostile opinion and the Bill was amended in such a manner that its very purpose was defeated.

HIS-27.claim: In 1905 Viceroy Curzon partitioned Bengal, separating East Bengal and merging it with Assam.
HIS-27.quote: In 1905, Viceroy Curzon partitioned Bengal. The British argued for dividing Bengal for reasons of administrative convenience. Even so, instead of removing the non-Bengali areas from the province, the government separated East Bengal and merged it with Assam.

HIS-27.claim: The Muslim League was formed at Dacca in 1906; its demand for separate electorates for Muslims was conceded by the government in 1909.
HIS-27.quote: A group of Muslim landlords and nawabs formed the All India Muslim League at Dacca in 1906. The League supported the partition of Bengal. It desired separate electorates for Muslims, a demand conceded by the government in 1909.

HIS-27.claim: In 1870 Viceroy Lord Mayo ensured provincial administrations received due share of revenue (financial decentralisation).
HIS-27.quote: In 1870 viceroy Lord Mayo ensured that all parts of provincial administration received due share of revenue to meet their needs.

HIS-27.claim: The Councils Act of 1909 introduced for the first time a representative element with elected non-official members, and separate representation for the Muslim community.
HIS-27.quote: The scope of political institutions in the provinces was expanded a little further following the introduction of Council of India Act, 1909. This Act introduced for the first time a "representative element" in British India, which included elected non-official members. This Act also introduced separate representation to Muslim community.

HIS-27.claim: The Government of India Act 1919 devolved authority to provinces, divided subjects and revenues between centre and provinces, and split provincial subjects into transferred and reserved.
HIS-27.quote: The Government of India Act 1919 devolved some authority to the provincial governments, retaining the control of the central government (unitary government) on them. It divided the subjects for jurisdiction of administration and sources of revenue between centre and provinces. The provincial subjects were divided into "transferred" and "reserved" categories.

HIS-27.claim: The Rowlatt Act (1919) curbed fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and strengthened police powers; Gandhi called a satyagraha against it in 1919.
HIS-27.quote: In 1919, Gandhiji gave a call for a satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act that the British had just passed. The Act curbed fundamental rights such as the freedom of expression and strengthened police powers.

HIS-27.claim: In 1927 the British government sent a commission headed by Lord Simon to decide India's political future; it had no Indian representative and all political groups decided to boycott it.
HIS-27.quote: In 1927, the British government in England decided to send a commission headed by Lord Simon to decide India's political future. The Commission had no Indian representative. The decision created an outrage in India. All political groups decided to boycott the Commission.

HIS-27.claim: The Nehru Report (1928) was the first attempt by Indians themselves to prepare a Constitution of India; it was named after its drafting committee chairman Motilal Nehru.
HIS-27.quote: The first attempt by Indians themselves to prepare a Constitution of India was made in the Nehru Report (1928). The Nehru Report was known as such because it was named after the chairman of its drafting committee, Motilal Nehru.

HIS-27.claim: The Government of India Act 1935 provided for provincial governments enjoying provincial autonomy.
HIS-27.quote: the Government of India Act, 1935 also provided for provincial government enjoying provincial autonomy.

HIS-27.claim: The 1935 Act provided three lists of power division (federal, concurrent, provincial) and a federal court to adjudicate federation-province disputes.
HIS-27.quote: This Act also provided for three lists of divisions of power between the federation (central government) and provinces: federal (central), concurrent and provincial. The Act also provided for establishment of a federal court to adjudicate disputes between federation and provinces.

HIS-27.claim: The 1935 federation could not be formed for want of princely unanimity; provincial elections were held in 1937 and Congress governments were formed in eight provinces (IGNOU).
HIS-27.quote: the federal government could not be formed because there was no unanimity among the princes to join the federation. And election to the provincial legislature as per the Government of India Act, 1935 was held in 1937. Following the election of 1937, provincial governments headed by the Indian National Congress were formed in eight provinces.

HIS-27.claim: NCERT records that the 1935 Act prescribed provincial autonomy, elections to provincial legislatures were announced for 1937, and Congress formed governments in 7 of 11 provinces.
HIS-27.quote: The combined struggles of the Indian people bore fruit when the Government of India Act of 1935 prescribed provincial autonomy and the government announced elections to the provincial legislatures in 1937. The Congress formed governments in 7 out of 11 provinces.

HIS-27.claim: In 1942 the British government sent cabinet member Sir Stafford Cripps with draft proposals on constitution-making.
HIS-27.quote: In 1942, the British government sent its cabinet member - Sir Stafford Cripps with the draft declaration on proposals (regarding formation of constitution for Indians) to be implemented at the end of the WW II

HIS-27.claim: The Cabinet Mission consisted of three cabinet members - Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander - and its proposals were announced on 16 May 1946.
HIS-27.quote: It consisted of three cabinet members - Lord Pathic-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps and Mr. A.V. Alexander. It, however, made its own proposal which was announced simultaneously on 16 May, 1946 in England as well as in India.

HIS-27.claim: The Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946 and was boycotted by the Muslim League.
HIS-27.quote: when the Constituent Assembly first met on December 9, 1946, it was boycotted by the Muslim League, and it functioned without the participation of the Muslim League.

HIS-27.claim: India attained independence at the midnight of 14-15 August 1947; two nation-states, India and Pakistan, came into existence.
HIS-27.quote: At the hour of midnight on 14-15 August 1947, India attained independence. On 14-15 August 1947, not one but two nation-states came into existence - India and Pakistan.

HIS-27.claim: Under the Mountbatten Plan the princely states were free to join India or Pakistan.
HIS-27.quote: Under the Mountbatten Plan, the Princely states were free to join India or Pakistan.

HIS-27.claim: C. Rajagopalachari served as a member of the Interim Government of 1946 and as free India's first Indian Governor-General.
HIS-27.quote: C. Rajagopalachari, popularly known as Rajaji, served as member of the Interim Government of 1946 and as free India's first Indian Governor-General.

HIS-27.claim: After 1858 all powers to govern India vested in the Secretary of State for India, assisted by a fifteen-member council; in British India he was assisted by the Viceroy with an executive council.
HIS-27.quote: In the centralized structure of power which was introduced in the provinces, all powers to govern India vested in the Secretary of State for India (and through him in the Crown). He was assisted by a fifteen-member council of ministers. In British India, the Secretary of State of India was assisted by the Viceroy, who was assisted by an executive council.

HIS-27.claim: The early Congress wanted Legislative Councils made more representative and civil service examinations held in India as well, not just in London.
HIS-27.quote: It wanted the Legislative Councils to be made more representative, given more power, and introduced in provinces where none existed. For this purpose, it called for civil service examinations to be held in India as well, not just in London.

HIS-27.claim: Gandhi launched the Quit India movement in the middle of the Second World War, telling the British to quit India immediately.
HIS-27.quote: Mahatma Gandhi decided to initiate a new phase of movement against the British in the middle of the Second World War. The British must quit India immediately, he told them.
